desc:
The array nums is a mountain: strictly increasing up to a peak (which is neither the first nor the last element), then strictly decreasing. The same value may occur once on each slope.

Return the element of nums that is closest to target, that is, the value x minimizing |x - target|. If two different values are equally close, return the smaller one.

For example, for nums = [1, 4, 9, 6, 2] and target = 5 the values 4 and 6 are both at distance 1, so the answer is 4. Use O(log n) time.
constraints: nums is guaranteed to be a mountain array
hints: If nums were sorted, the closest value would be one of the two neighbours of the insertion point of target. Can you make the mountain look sorted?
The peak splits the mountain into an ascending part and a descending part. Each part is sorted, just in opposite directions.
Find the peak by binary search. In each part find the insertion position of target and look at the element just before and just after it. Compare at most 4 candidates by the pair (distance, value).
editorial: Closest-value search in a sorted array only needs the neighbours of where the target would be inserted. A mountain is two sorted arrays glued at the peak, so do the same twice.

First locate the peak index with the standard slope test. In the ascending part nums[0..peak] binary search the first index a with nums[a] ≥ target; the candidates are nums[a - 1] and nums[a] if they exist in that part. In the descending part nums[peak + 1..] binary search the first index a with nums[a] ≤ target; again the candidates are nums[a - 1] and nums[a].
Among at most four candidates choose the one with the smallest key (|x - target|, x), which implements the 'smaller value wins ties' rule. Three binary searches give O(log n) time and O(1) space.
